public_brief: Payroll prorates an employee's first pay period, and the platform team owns the math. Implement pay_period_split(period_start, period_end, hire_date). The period is one biweekly pay window given as two ISO date strings (YYYY-MM-DD); hire_date is the day the employee started, also ISO (YYYY-MM-DD). Answer one question: of the days in this pay period, how many are payable to this employee? Return a tuple (payable_days, total_days) of plain ints, where total_days is the size of the whole period regardless of the hire date. The grader imports your module and calls the function directly with routine windows and adversarial ones - hires on the edges, hires outside the window, malformed arguments - and compares return values exactly, so every input path needs one defined answer. Keep it a pure function: no printing, no file or network access, no clock reads.
entry_contract: Implement pay_period_split(period_start, period_end, hire_date) taking three ISO date strings and returning a tuple of two ints (payable_days, total_days).

hidden_spec.rule: Every calendar day in the period counts as a payable day - weekends and holidays included; payroll accrues daily, not per business day.
Both period endpoints are inclusive: a period running Monday to the Sunday fourteen days later spans exactly 14 days, and a one-day period where start equals end spans 1.
The hire date itself is a payable day - an employee hired on the period's last day earns that one day.
A hire date before period_start makes the entire period payable (payable equals total).
A hire date after period_end pays nothing - payable is 0 - and the comparison is strict, so a hire on the day right after the period still gets zero.
A period whose end is before its start is malformed and raises ValueError.
Any date argument that is not a YYYY-MM-DD string raises ValueError rather than being coerced or ignored.

answer_sheet.answer: Calendar days, all of them - weekends count, holidays count. Salaried folks accrue every single day of the period.
Both ends inclusive. Monday through the Sunday two weeks later is 14 days, not 13. A start equal to the end is a one-day period.
Your first day is a paid day. Start on the last day of the period and you still earned that day.
If they were on staff before the period opened, the whole period is theirs - no proration at all.
Joined after the period closed, zero payable days - and the day right after the period is still after, so still zero.
An end date before the start date is a data-entry bug; raise ValueError rather than quietly paying someone negative days.
Anything that won't parse as YYYY-MM-DD raises ValueError. Payroll would rather break loudly than cut a check off a guessed date.
Out of scope - this splits days, not hours; overtime lives in the time-tracking system.
Out of scope - no money math here; withholding is computed downstream from the day counts.

provenance.derivation: Rules derived from mainstream payroll proration practice - inclusive pay windows, daily accrual that counts weekends, first-day-payable hires, loud failure on malformed periods - not from any WiseCounsil design document.
